By means of the two-fold worship: Rudra and Rudrāṇī are the two Rudras; their *yāmala* is the form consisting of both joined together. *Siddhi* refers to both the external and internal [attainments], thus it is *oṃ*. As it has been said: "When the mind is restrained within dharma and adharma, then he speaks that which..."

"A mantra is powerful by its very nature; how much more so when it arises from the *mātṛkā*! And thus says the Śruti: "O Sarasvatī, whether you are uttered or unuttered, be auspicious to us, most peaceful, and most gracious; do not look upon us with hostility. O Sarasvatī—O Power whose essence is reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), inseparable from the Supreme Brahman—you who...

You are Speech (vāk), whose nature is the reflective awareness of consciousness, arisen as the manifest sound of the breath; you who are unarisen in the form of the Intermediate Speech (madhyamā), existing yet imperceptible to others; and you who are Auspicious (śivā), whose form is the Visionary Speech (paśyantī), free from contact with suffering due to the supreme nature of the reflective awareness of the conscious self. And you who...

You are the most peaceful, indeed, because you are a mass of bliss (*ānandaghana*) and possess the supreme form (*parārūpa*). May you, as such, be perceived by us as one who is exceedingly gracious, becoming the worldly consciousness-bliss (*laukikacidānanda*).
Likewise, may the wound in your own nature—characterized by the forgetting of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the space-consciousness-self (*vyomacidātman*)—be healed in all four [states].
I have spoken of you, I have touched you, and I have seen you; through the direct realization of your true nature, may I remain forever free from affliction—this is our aspiration.
Thus ends the *Śrīparātriṃśikāvivṛti* composed by Rājānaka Lakṣmīrāma. It was written on the eleventh day of the month of Kārttika in the year 43.

The *Triṃśikā* (The Thirty) so called because it expresses the three powers—will, knowledge, and action—not because of a conjunction of thirty [verses], for even this much constitutes the meaning of the *Triṃśikā*; for thus it is said in the *Śrītantrasaura*: "The meaning of the *Triṃśikā* has been proclaimed by you."
The expansion of all ten million [verses] is as follows: Oṃ, homage to the glorious Mahāgāyatrī.

Oṃ. That which is the object of knowledge, that which is the effect, the world that is desirable, that which is to be manifested, the knower, the agent, the will, and the supreme that is to be manifested—all this is indeed not other than the manifesting subject;
for the entire multitude of existing things has as its very body the will, knowledge, action, and the "I-consciousness."
Victory to that true, supreme Lordly Light, whose nature is the reflective awareness of consciousness, which is extracted from its own essential form!

The three-peaked Sundarī, who shines eternally in the heart as the manifest form of the worship of the Three Worlds through ritual action, devotion, study, reflection, and meditative absorption— may she kindly grant me an unobstructed ear for even a moment to the sequence of arranging the preceding meanings within her seed-syllables.
If the world [is that] for which they have compassion.

In this context, indeed, there was first a certain primordial nature established as consisting of vibration (spanda), which is beyond the supreme mind, beyond the ego, beyond movement, beyond vital breath, beyond body, and beyond consciousness. By its own will, it acted in order to unfold the transformations such as bliss, desire, and seeking, which are to be described hereafter.

From that which is independent, pure, free, and of a non-manifest nature, is there not admitted a vibration (*spanda*) consisting of subtle movement? That very [vibration], in its form as total acceptance, is the syllable *Oṃ*.
Prajāpati describes that very reality of *Oṃ*, in which all phenomenal expansion has completely subsided, just as [in the verse beginning] "nā... [the *Nādabindu Upaniṣad*].
Non-being existed; at that time, being did not exist. There was neither the dust of the earth nor the sky beyond it.
Thus, there was neither death nor the mortal; there was no sign of night or day. That One breathed, windless, by its own inherent power (*svadhayā*). Other than that, nothing else existed beyond it.

In the beginning, there was nothing whatsoever; this entire world was hidden by darkness, an ocean enveloped in gloom. Only the breath of life existed, that which was covered by the void. Then, the Will arose, the first seed of mind. Upon its arising, the light of existence was born below it. Who knows, who here can declare it? Did the gods come into being after this? Time’s vast expanse lies beyond this world; whether it exists or does not exist—only he who surveys it in the highest heaven knows, or perhaps even he does not know.
The meaning of the word here is "itself."

In the state of the realization of emptiness, there was no cognition such as "the jar does not exist," nor was there a cognition such as "this is a real jar" adorned by the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*), because the world of *rajas* did not exist.

Neither the sky, nor anything else such as fire, water, and so forth existed previously; even death did not exist, for there was no refuge from death, and consequently, there was no birth. At that time, there was neither night nor day. He shows what did exist at that time with the words beginning "Then there was..."—that which is non-dual.

By its own inherent power (*svadhayā*), which is the very nature of self-sustenance, it brought forth that which is pure consciousness of the object—changing the case ending for the sake of the meter—as the form of food (*annarūpam*).
It brought forth even the mind consisting of food (*annamaya-manas*) as the form of food; it brought forth the windless and breathless state.
That [Being] became the breath (*prāṇa*); being without food, it became the life-force (*prāṇana*) and the very life of the breath, and likewise the life of the mind.
The meaning is that the reality which is the mind was itself that [reality].
For another scriptural passage states: "They know that which is the life of life, the eye of the eye, the ear of the ear, and the mind of the mind.
And from the text, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," there exists the knowledge of whether something is or is not, which enters the path of deliberation.
And since that *śānti* (peace) is beyond verbal definition, it is designated by the word "darkness" (*tamas*) because of its unassailable nature.
Thus, in passages such as "In the beginning there was darkness hidden by darkness," it means that even though it was pure and non-dual, it became darkness;
and from that darkness [all else arose].

There was no knowledge. If one asks why, it has been said in response to that: "If there were someone by whom even a mere atom did not exist, then indeed there was only darkness; otherwise, how could the well-spoken statement 'there was darkness' be logically consistent?"

Enveloped by darkness, there was concealment; even darkness was not within the range of experience. Otherwise, that which has been stated—that "nothing else whatsoever existed beyond it"—would not have occurred, because from that indefinable reality (tattva), no other thing whatsoever [could exist]. Indeed, it is well known that nothing else whatsoever [existed] beyond it.
The meaning is that for no one was there non-existence; the intention is that even if everything were absent, if there were only darkness, then how could one say "there is nothing at all"?

Now, one might object: "If at that time the universe did not exist, then how could the expansion of reality (tattvaprapañca) have emerged from that which was devoid of the universe? For how can something emerge from where it was not present? Anticipating this doubt, he states by way of another perspective that the universe existed there, and refutes [the objection] by saying "it is not so," [concluding]: "All was a mere sign (praketa), a single expanse of water."

"Idam" (this) refers to the state prior to the desire for manifold manifestation; at first, the universe was slightly of the nature of *rasa* (flavor/essence). But immediately after that desire, all this visible world became as a whole a body of water (*salila*), characterized by a pre-eminent stability (*praketa*) and fixed in the form of *rasa*. Here, *rasa* also signifies *sneha* (affection/cohesion), and that too is of the very nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*).
The universe existed as the essence of consciousness (*cidrasa*).

Indeed, it was swollen in the form of the visible and became gross; for it is said that in the beginning and at the end it is of the nature of the essence of consciousness, while in the middle it is of the nature of a bubble of the essence of consciousness. Such is its state.
For even in states such as deep sleep, meditative absorption (*samādhi*), or fainting, the body, vital breath, intellect, and so forth are indeed perceived;

however, the absence of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) regarding [objects] such as blue or internal pleasure is well-known to all people. Thus, the established meaning is that the syllable *Oṃ* is the reality of Brahman (*brahmatattva*). As it has been said: "He who is the form of the Unsurpassable (*anuttara*), by his own will..."

"That vibration (*spanda*) by which this entire world is perceived is called the first *Śivatattva* by those who know it. This very state of primordial manifestation (*ādyākṛtadaśā*) is also shown in the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* through the Vedas: "Who indeed here knows that primordial source from which arose the Ṛṣi, at the time when both gods and demons were born?"
Neither existence nor non-existence, nor both, nor even the flow of time exists here; nothing at all remains, for everything has been consumed by Your fire.

From such a source— a most pure universal form (viśvarūpa) consisting of subtle essence (rasa), which possesses the aspect of the universal (sāmānya) while being devoid of the aspect of the particular (viśeṣa)— there arose in Kāmākhya a specific desire (icchāviśeṣa) that was entirely of the nature of water and even purer than that. That too...
The nature [of Śiva] is "May I become many, may I procreate," according to the principle that "I am alone, I shall eat [the world].
This reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which rests solely in its own essential nature as light, has no other object;
it consists in resting in the self-luminosity of one's own Self. This "I-consciousness" (*ahamartha*) is the Śiva-tattva.

The *oṃkāra* is the resting in self-luminosity that does not turn toward anything else; it is consciousness itself, consisting of *cidānanda* (consciousness-bliss) and consisting of the very nature of the manifestation of the universe. When that consciousness undergoes a slight swelling (*ucchūnatā*), it takes the form of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) and becomes the seed-ground of all entities, established through that power.
At the beginning of the recitation of mantras, the two principles of Śakti and Śiva are indeed represented by the two syllables *oṃ* and *ka*.

According to the *Yāmala* tradition, with the intention of denoting the light (*prakāśa*) whose nature is pure consciousness, the syllable *oṃ* is Śiva-tattva; and with the intention of denoting the self-reflective awareness (*ahaṃvimarśa*), it is Śakti. This is what is meant.

From that pure consciousness— which is perfectly full within, whose face is turned toward the exterior, which is indivisible, and which is of a single uniform flavor— there appeared water in the form of rasa, characterized by the desire to emerge outwardly.

In this land of Kaśmīra, on a certain mountain peak that is always desolate, during the spring and summer seasons when the waters flow abundantly, at the time of twilight, [the sound] "Oṃ ka" arrives— just as one might say "the first threshing"— this is the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*); the application to the subject (*dārṣṭāntika*), however, is as follows:
The mass of colors illuminating the source of desire (*kāmayoni*) and so forth indicates an external covering by virtue of the expansion of the power of the autonomous Consciousness-Kāmeśvara; thus,
although the disclosure of the secret meaning of the mantra is unfit for ordinary people, it is here made clear for their sake.
Thinking that it would cause an obstruction to the disciples, let these excellent worshippers—their inner hearts pierced by the descent of Śiva’s power (śaktipāta)—hold this for themselves. (p.
4) However, we shall not clarify the meaning of the aforementioned analogy regarding each seed at this point.
Both [points] will become clear through the explanation of the meaning of the mantra. *Kaṃjala* refers to that which is called *kāma*; *kaṃ* is the head of the two dogs (*aśunaḥ*).
In the *Prajāpati-sūkta*, Prajāpati spoke of the manifestation of the desire of the power of consciousness: "In the beginning, there was that desire."

"From the two minds, the seed first came into being"—therefore, from that which was prior to all non-existence, *kāma* (desire), the letter *ka*, came into being (*samavartata*) or was born, for the purpose of becoming manifold. When the question "from what? arises, it says: "that which was the first thing."

He is the primordial cause of the mind, which consists of conceptualization and discursive thought; and it is stated in another Purāṇa: "The Noble One created the waters alone; from them He emitted that seed of great potency, which became the golden egg, radiant with a thousand rays."
Water is the object of generality; desire is the essence; the passion for manifold becoming is the will;

the capacity for the discernment of "I am this" and so forth is vigor; power is Māyā; and the fourfold cosmic egg, characterized by earth and other elements, is golden—that is, composed of gold characterized by supreme luminosity.

O Lord, your radiance is equal to the sun because the staff consists of supreme light; there is merely a slight perspiration, yet entirely free from any particular sweat, a state of intense density arising from the manifestation of that [light], a state of profoundest darkness.
Gradually, the subtle essence of consciousness itself transforms into the form of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) and the individual body (bhairavāṇḍa);

this manifestation of grossness from the subtle remains an object of universal experience even today, as seen in the development of the soft semen-drop— composed of the five elements— once cast into the womb, becoming an embryo (kalila).
This is because we observe a sequence of transformations, such as from the stage of a bubble to that of a solid mass,
and so forth; likewise, the transformation of water— which is essentially fluid— into a crystal gem over time through a gradual process,
and the transformation of a seed and the like into a sprout, then into a sap, branches, trunk, and so on, are also observed.
This was stated by the venerable Ācārya through the hymn of praise to the deity.

"The congealed flood of the essence of consciousness, having attained a state of formal manifestation, appears to me as my own direct experience in the form of the universe— this is the body of Bhairava."

With the intention that space and the other elements are essentially of the nature of pure consciousness (*cidghana*), even the followers of the Upaniṣads have stated that Brahman alone is the cause of space and the rest; thus says the Taittirīya Upaniṣad:
"From this very Self, space was produced; from space, air; from air, fire; from fire, water..."

"From the first [Agni] comes the earth; from the earth, the plants; from the plants, food," and so forth. Furthermore, whatever entire world is seen or even heard, whether internal or external—all that Nārāyaṇa stands pervading.
Thus, by the proclamation of the Taittirīyas, the seed cast into the womb, having pervaded both internally and externally, remains as the living soul consisting of pure consciousness.
There is no disagreement whatsoever on this point.
However, for up to three months or even four months, there is a lack of clarity regarding the movement of the *jīva*,
but not its absence; thereafter, from the very month in which the vibration of the *jīva* becomes manifest,
the independent conscious Self (*svatantra-cidātman*), as the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*), performs the activity of the vibration of consciousness, which is then perceived.

Let every person be attentive to this: through the very act of vibration becoming solidified by means of postures (*āsanas*), space (*ākāśa*)—which is characterized by vacuity—gradually arises within the domain of the internal organs.
Is it not the case that space is produced from the Supreme Lord? Indeed, it is produced; such is the experience of all.
Regarding the arising of space: it is true that the arising of space delimited by the interior of a seed or a drop occurs through the action of vibration (*spandana*).
But if one asks how the arising of the external great space (*mahākāśa*) occurs from the Supreme Lord, [the answer is:
even the great space shines forth from the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*), which is the source of all manifestations; this is the seat of the birth of space.
The generation of space has consciousness as its agent; "by its light all this shines"—such is the Upaniṣad.
Therefore, it is said: "From the Self, space was produced. For without the vibration of consciousness, the manifestation of space could not first occur there.
Since there is an absence of any void due to its nature as the essence of the flavor of *vindu*, enough with this elaboration.

Even for one for whom agency is directly stated to exist in ether, air, fire, water, and earth, nevertheless, it is the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*)— the agent of action within consciousness conditioned by ether and the other elements— who is the cause of ether and the rest, because they are insentient (*jaḍatvena*).

Because there is no independence [in this case], so too have the venerable Bhāratītīrtha-pādas said: "When it is stated that 'the Lord rules from within,' Brahman, having space and so forth as its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), would be the cause of speech and the rest; for even fire and the other elements are seen to proceed from air.
If this is so, then how is the arrangement regarding the agency of the elements—such as "from space comes air, from air comes fire," and so on—to be explained?
If it is argued that [this] has been constructed because the conceptualization of an adjunct (*upādhi*) is impossible once the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) has been abandoned, we reply:
this is for the purpose of making the experience known. For such is the experience of everyone:
in the absence of space, there is an absence of vibration, as in the case of bamboo, reeds, and the like when subjected to an extremely powerful wind.

The friction of two objects against one another does not produce fire; however, in the case of the subtle production of fire, there is an intensification of the flame through the blowing of air from the mouth. When the heat of the sun increases, perspiration arises from the body;
and when internal heat from fever or other causes increases, sweat-water is produced. This is the result: it is consciousness alone [that manifests in these forms].
It has become condensed through the manifestation of the phenomenal world, such as space and so forth.
As it is stated in the *Mahārāmāyaṇa*, in the dialogue concerning the Ikṣvāku lineage:

In this regard, everything was, is, and will be equal, peaceful, the eternal and imperishable object of consciousness, boundless, and without appearance— neither blind darkness, nor the darkness below destruction, nor light, nor anything else whatsoever; for by its nature as the single essence of pure consciousness, it is indeed all that exists.

By the Supreme Lord—who is himself free from beginning, end, and middle, and who is not a product of volition—there was no volition conceived; yet he remained as the self whose nature is volition, the light of the mind, and the unborn. (p.
7) By him, through the mind, this vast body of space was volitionally created; and from the density of the mind and space, [the world arose].

The wind, having become fully developed and throbbing through its union with the air of the mental ether, then perceived light; subsequently, it took on the form of volition consisting of the nature of a portion of fire, and thereafter water was established.
That mass of the four elements, by virtue of the swelling of the mind-egg, remained as an egg, which then became the lotus-born Brahmā.
Behold the two worlds as perfected; there, this great world, including Meru and the rest, exists as a mere appearance of parts.
Thus, Brahman alone is perceived as all-pervasive, yet it appears as if possessed of modification through its vibrations, such as the transformations of existence and so forth.
In the *Phāṇḍogya* as well, for this very reason, the established conclusion is: "All this, indeed, is Brahman; it is dissolved in Him.

If it is asked what the purpose of the creation of space (*ākāśa*) is, independence (*svātantrya*) is the cause here. Furthermore, regarding that which was previously nothing but the unmanifest Self, what is the proof for its existence?
If it is argued that this is because the knower of that [world] is also incapable of knowing it in the absence of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), it is replied:

First, the Vedāntic statements such as "In the beginning, this was Being alone" (*sadeva somyedam*) are the supreme authority; subsequently, the scripture regarding the awakening from sleep—such as the rising of one who was lying on his face—is also an authority, for [this occurs] even in the absence of deep sleep, meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and so forth.
Someone who does not reflect upon the body, vital breath, intellect, and so forth within their own self might deny that very self, thinking, "I was not there; that was someone else.
However, one thinks, "I slept with my face [downward]; I was conscious of nothing."

The experience of the face-bed (mukha-śayana) and the experience of ignorance are not of the present time; at the beginning of creation, the primordial, unsurpassed state of consciousness (cittatva-sattva) awakens. How so? Just as during times such as sleep or fainting, even though there is an absence of knowledge, at the time of awakening there is the recollection of prior awareness and the vision of the manifestation through the gateway of memory.
Just as it was previously, even now, in the absence of the cognition of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), it is impossible to negate the existence of the cognizer;

otherwise, if the Witness (*sākṣin*) were not present during states such as knowledge or sleep, how could there be the first-person reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) "I slept" and the subsequent memory? Therefore, the apprehension of the Self’s eternity must be accepted; thus, the conscious Self (*cidātman*) is eternal.
It is established.

Now, why is it that you do not prescribe the recitation of the *gāyatrī* itself for one who has been born as a Brahmin? [The answer is: Because of the statement, "There is nothing to be recited beyond the *gāyatrī*," it is impossible to abandon the deliberation on the mantra beginning with "Savitṛ, Bharga, Devasya, Dhiyo Yo Naḥ. Why, then, [is this] the *gāyatrī* mantra [recited] at the time of initiation (*upanayana*)?

If one asks why the recitation begins with "Oṃ Ka," etc., setting aside what was taught first, the answer is: true, even in this case there is no harm whatsoever. That very Brahma-veda which teaches the preeminence of the Gāyatrī also connects the Saubhāgyavidyā with it as being one and the same; for indeed, in the Atharva-veda...

The *praṇava* was emitted by the foot of Savitṛ, and the letter *ka* by the word *bharga*; thus, because there is no difference between Gāyatrī and Sundarī, there is only a difference in name and not a difference in substance. Listen to the *Tripuropaniṣad* as declared in the Vedas by Bhṛgu and Aṅgiras; for therein, first of all, begins "That [splendor] of Savitṛ," and so forth.

Having first performed the joining of the feet of the three-footed Gāyatrī with "parorajasi sā vadoṃ," others then recite the mantra for Jātavedas, followed by the *tryambaka* kūṭa; thus the Gāyatrī mantra is proclaimed to possess the nature of Tripura,
beginning from "tat savituḥ" and ending with "amṛtāt," consisting of one hundred and eight syllables.

The mantra of Śatākṣarā Sundarī is revealed in the Śrauta [scriptures]. As it is stated there: "Śatākṣarī is the supreme knowledge consisting of the three Vedas; she is the eight-syllabled Tripurā Parameśvarī. The first four words are the manifestations of the Supreme Brahman; the second set is called Śākta, and the third is Śaiva. The Vedas, the Śāstras, the Purāṇas, the codes of Dharma, the medical sciences, and the luminaries—all these are understood to be formed through the union of Śiva and Śakti; this is the meaning of such passages as "consisting of the three" (tayīmāyī) and so forth. For example: *ka-dhra-traṃ*, *le-kūṭaṃ*, *has-ādi-kūṭaṃ*, and *sā-di-kūṭaṃ*—according to the Tantric tradition, these constitute the Tripurā mantra.

In the same way, this Supreme Goddess Tripurā, according to the path of the Vedas, consists of the threefold Veda (*trayī*), consists of the three *kūṭas*, and consists of the mantras of Bharga, Brahmā, Śakti, and Śiva. Here too, beginning with *tat* and ending with *sā vadoṃ*, the first *kūṭa* is for Jātavedas.

Beginning with "agniriti" and ending with "antaṃ" constitutes the second peak (kūṭa); following that, from "tryasvakam" to "māmṛtāt" constitutes the third peak. Thus, there are one hundred and eight syllables (*valāḥ*). Here, the collective meaning of this Vedic mantra is as follows: first is the conscious sun (*cidarka*) in the form of light (*prakāśa*), and subsequently is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
Immediately following that is the contemplation of the two-fold creation consisting of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge.

The world consists of fourteen types of elemental creation (*bhautika-sarga*), as stated by the Sāṅkhyas: the divine class is of eightfold variety, the animal and plant kingdom is fivefold, and the human class is of one kind;
or alternatively, it consists of fourteen types comprising the seven worlds beginning with Bhūr and the subterranean regions beginning with Atala and Vitala.

The names of these thirty-six sages are as follows: Manu, Gautama, Saṃvarta, Viṣṇu, Śātātapa, and Kaśyapa.
