The medical treatises on Āyurveda, such as the Vārāhī, the Bṛhajjātaka, the Sūryabrahmavaṭeśvara-siddhānta, the Kurūhala, and others.

Śiva is illumination (*prakāśa*) and Śakti is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); from their union, characterized by aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*), the entire phenomenal world arises as consisting of Śiva and Śakti (p. 10). Now, by means of the word *tat*, through the reference to the letter *ka*, that which is proclaimed in the *Tripuropaniṣad* is shown: "Now, in this interval, the supreme..."
We shall explain the *Gahvara*: that which has arisen from the Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*) is the eternal Brahman.

The Supreme Lord—devoid of characteristics (*nirlakṣaṇa*), stainless (*nirañjana*), free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*), and without affliction (*ādhirahita*)—the God, rolls up, beholds, and expands;
He desires that state of consciousness (*caitanya-bhāva*). That very God, in the form of Śiva, exists as the object of vision.

He expands within ascetics, in sacrifices, and among yogis; he desires desire at will, and as one who desires desire, he is born. A woman is born, and he creates the letters *ka, ca, ṭa, pa, ya, śa, and na*; that desire is born as the stainless one (*nirañjana*). Desire unfolds through the state of desire; that is the god Kāmadeva, the pervasive one. Thus, he grasps the letter *ka*, which is the meaning of that word.
Regarding the phrase "speak thus," this is the meaning of the sentence here.

The Great Mantra, the Great Incantation, beginning with "Tat savitur vareṇyam" and so forth—arisen from that, which is the manifest word "Tat," that should be known as the eternal Brahman, unmanifest, stainless, and beginningless. He alone is the Supreme God; being initially desireless, by His own will, through a descent into the state of consciousness, He desires the object of desire.

Thus, the Supreme Lord unfolds as the object of desire and arises in the form of the visible world; therefore, that very Brahman is the letter *ka*. In the first two quarters of the Sāvitrī mantra, that Brahman—which is without desire and without action—is declared by the word *bharga* to be the object of meditation. However, in the third quarter, by virtue of its impelling power, it becomes active and endowed with reflective awareness (*savimarśa*).

In the *Saubhāgyavidyā* proclaimed by Brahmā, the reality (*tattva*) consisting of the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which takes the form of desire (*kāmarūpa*), is indicated by the letter *ka* at its beginning. One should understand that there is indeed identity between that word and the word "desire" (*kāma*). Just as in the *Kādividya*, so it is also in the *Gāyatrī* mantra.

(p. 11) Consisting of Śiva and Śakti, the Gāyatrī meter—relative to its twenty-four syllables—is feminine in gender by means of the suffix *ī*, like the Vṛhatī or Jagatī meters; thus it possesses the nature of Śakti in its state as a mantra, whereas in its objective state, it is denoted by the terms Bharga and Arka, whose essence is luminosity.

The state of being Śiva arises through the power of meditating on and describing the forms of the Impeller (Pracodaka) and the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin); and how this is so has been explained in the *Satkṛtagāyatrīmantravivaraṇa* by the statement "creation is to be enjoined. Enough with this digression; we shall now explain the subject at hand.

In this context, within the *śakti-tattva*, there will subsequently arise the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of many states as one; thus, within the womb of *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), in the letter *ka*— which is of the nature of water, consists of *icchā* (will), and is denoted by the word "many" (*bahu*)— there exists the subtle aspect of consciousness (*cidaṃśa*), whose essence is the "I" (*idantā*), which is of the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*) and *śakti*.

And that conscious aspect known as the Śiva-tattva, which consists of the form of light and is of the nature of "I" (ahaṃ-rūpa), is included within this [root *jan*]; likewise, according to the dual meaning of the verbal root *jan*,
there is the conscious aspect consisting of action (*kriyā-rūpa*) through the manifestation of the agent (*sartā*), which is termed "multifarious ideation" (*bahubhāvanā*).

When these three components, which are of the nature of *rasa*, become solidified (*ghanībhūta*), then the pure Will (*śuddhecchā*)—in the form of the letters of the corners consisting of Knowledge and Action—is brought down for the practitioner. At the time of recitation, [the sequence is]: *e*, *i*, *dhra*; then *ā*, *tā*, *va*, *dā*, *gataṃ*;
*toṃ*, *ka*, *dhra*. Here, in the sphere of the object of desire (*eṣṭavya*) and the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), they appear in this order.
The repose of will, knowledge, and action occurs in this state; at this time,

when Śiva and Īśvara have pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) as their instrument, the powers of will, knowledge, and action clearly arise in the form "I know all this" and "I do all this," through the grasping of the state of the letter *e*.

According to the followers of the Nārada Pañcarātra system, who are the foremost among the Sāttvata devotees, the syllable *A* is the Lord Viṣṇu as Vāsudeva in his wise form; the emanation (vyūha) beginning with Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others resides therein in a subtle state.
One should contemplate the density of the letter *a* itself as the letter *ka* and so forth. The letter *ka* is the manifestation (*vyūha*) of Vāsudeva;
it is the first transformation of the conscious Vāsudeva, consisting of the manifestations of Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha.
It is the creation of all individual souls (*jīva*) endowed with all internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Vāsudeva dwells within the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, and Vāsudeva [himself] also dwells [therein].

According to the Taittirīya Śruti, "Nārāyaṇa stands pervading all that exists, both within and without," first the Lord, who is free from desire, became solidified through the transformation of the syllable *a* (the essence of will) into the syllable *e*.
From that emerged the individual soul (*jīva*), mind (*manas*), and ego (*ahaṅkāra*). This triad of manifestations is the syllable *ekāra*; thus, it is *ekāra*.

The three letters are the corners of the *kalā*; the first corner is *śuddhi*, the second corner is *manas*, and the third is *ahaṃkāra*. Thus, the letter *e* denotes the collection of these three manifestations (*vyūha*).
This very point has also been stated in the Jñānālaya.
They say that from the letter *e* arises the Vaiṣṇavī power, which is intent upon the protection of the universe.

According to that view, the meaning of this great mantra (*oṃ tatsaviturvareṇyam*) is as follows: *oṃ tat* refers to the one called Vāsudeva, the *savitṛ* (impeller) of Savitṛ, who consists of the fourfold manifestation (*caturvyūha*), the progenitor and producer of all creation and the multitude of living beings.

We meditate upon the entire syllable *E*, which is most excellent, supreme, imperishable, and luminous; which has the form of the *bhaga* and the nature of the triangle of creation (*sarga*); which belongs to the Lord Vāsudeva;
and which is the transformation of the conscious Vāsudeva known as the mind, the intellect, and the ego—indeed, we contemplate it all for the purification of the mind.

The *ṛ* and *ṣa* are in the genitive case according to Vedic usage; thus, the *Tripuropaniṣad* states: "She who gives birth to living beings, whose power is the primordial *Tripurā-śakti*—this *Tripurā*, the Supreme Goddess, the Great *Kuṇḍalinī*, the Goddess, is the power of the triangle through the letter *E*."
Since it was produced by the illustrious one in the form of the *bhaga*, therefore the single syllable (*ekākṣara*) alone is taken;
that which is most excellent (*vareṇya*), best, worthy of worship, and to be saluted—therefore, in the word "vareṇya," the single syllable is understood. If this is so...
The first line, connected with the letter *e* and beginning from the left side extending to the right side, is the first city;
the second is the second city, the body; and the third body is on the right side.
The third line, variegated by its downward orientation from the top, begins from the left side and merges with the lower portion; thus, the Supreme Goddess, consisting of the three cities,
is the Triangular Power (Trikoṇa-Śakti), the Great Kuṇḍalinī, coiled in the form of a spiral comprising all the enclosures.
The body is the root.
The three channels named Kuṇḍalinī, also called the letter E, are the powers of Tripurā; they take the form of three lines and the form of three coils.
[What is] the union of these three coils? *?

If it is asked, "What is the meaning of the word *kuṇḍalinī*?", listen: according to the system of Yoga, first there is a region called the *kanda-sthāna*, located above the genitals and below the navel;
therein resides a single channel (*nāḍī*) named the support of all channels (*sarvanāḍī*), which exists in all classes of living beings as the intestinal coil (*antraveṣṭanikā*).
The syllable *oṃ* is like the curling of hair, resembling the form of a whirlpool or a conch-shell,
and similar in shape to a sleeping lord of serpents; it remains in an unbroken, circular coil, floating day and night,
and within that very center lies the power of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) moving with a subtle motion.
She, who is the cause of all vibrations, exists in the form of Kuṇḍalinī like a coiled serpent;

because she resides within the body, and because the support and the supported are metaphorically treated as non-different—just as the Person (Puruṣa) residing in the heart, though only the size of a thumb, is described as "thumb-sized" in the Vedic text: "The Person is of the measure of a thumb."

The vital energy (prāṇa-śakti) known as Kuṇḍalinī consists of the three cities named Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumṇā. According to the perspective of phenomenal appearance (prātītika-mata), however, that which bestows existence upon the vital breath, impels it, and generates its ascent and descent is the power of the reflective awareness of consciousness (cid-vimarśa-śakti); she is Mahākuṇḍalinī, who resides within the three cities known as the gross, subtle, and causal.

p. 14) And she, being identical with those [three], is to be sought: as desire in the form of the object of desire (*iṣṭa*), as the object of knowledge in the form of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), and as action in the form of the effect (*kārya*). Thus Tripurā, known as Consciousness (*caitanya*), is to be meditated upon;
because she is coiled (*kuṇḍalita*), she is called Kuṇḍalinī. All of this is set forth in the Mahārāmāyaṇa as follows:
Circular in shape, residing in the region of the *kanda*, having the form of intestinal coils,
supported by hundreds of channels and sub-channels, resembling the whorl at the end of a lute, like a whirlpool in water,
established in the form of the syllable *Oṃ* of the scripts and so forth, and situated like a spiral coil among gods, asuras, and humans.

Among all living beings— from deer, crocodiles, and birds down to insects and those born from lotuses— the serpent king, afflicted by the cold, lies asleep; his body is encircled by the Lord, and through the opening at the base of the navel, he appears bright like the moon melting away due to the fire of the white [subtle] body moving by the force of its own activity, bound in a coil.

Constantly floating as if by the vibrations of the vital essence, she remains within that [body], as tender as the interior of a plantain tree; as long as the power of the wind manifests, she vibrates with a graceful movement like a flute.
Flowing in a coiled form, she is called by the name Kuṇḍalinī—the supreme power of living beings, the conqueror of all powers.
"Constantly emitting sighs as if angry, standing still with her face turned away, she has become the cause of all throbbings.
Thus, by this [verse] beginning with "Oṃ Ka," the meaning of the first two quarters of the Gāyatrī has been shown; now, the meaning of the third quarter—

Intending to unify with the letters of the second and third *kūṭas*, which are accompanied by the first *kūṭa* situated as *tri-l-hrīṃ*— characterized by being the impeller of the intellect of all beings from Sadāśiva down to an insect—
the author speaks of the expansion of the triangle of pure Will, Knowledge, and Action, which is the abode of many worlds, using the syllables *tri-le-rgi*.

Thus, Tripurā-śakti, whose form consists of three corners produced by two seed-syllables (*bīja*) and who has the shape of the *bhaga*, requires the emission of *vīrya* into the *yoni*; for *vīrya* is, in effect, the sovereignty known as *śānta* with respect to the infinite objects of desire, knowledge, and action. (p. 15)
The power to perform the divine play of creating, not performing, or acting otherwise resides in the blessed Kāmeśvarī, who is the essence of Tripurā;
the blessed Kāmeśvara enters into her.
Even Vāsudeva himself, an incarnation of Kāmeśvarī, sings: "My womb is the Great Brahman; in it..."
"I shall conceive a fetus."

The Great Brahman is the great power of reflection (*vimarśa-śakti*) in the form of a triangle; the meaning is that within that triangular *ekāra*, I bestow the potency of consciousness (*cid-vīrya*) known as "I am this.
Following the threefold contemplation, through the manifestation of infinite objects of desire and so forth, by means of those objects...

The letter *Ī* has arisen as the manifestation of the excellence of sovereignty (*aiśvaryātiśaya*). *Ī* signifies ruling (*īśana*), that is to say, sovereignty; thus, the letter *Ī* is named Īśāna. The letter *L* is Lekharṣabha (Indra), who is distinguished by supreme sovereignty and endowed with manifold prosperity.
Just as in the world, the production of a fetus occurs through the emission of semen into the womb, so too here [is it produced].
The infinite categories of objects— such as the pure, the horse, the self, the knowable, and so forth— are known through that [consciousness]. Regarding those objects,

there is the constant imposition of "mineness" (*mamatā*) by means of the unfolding of the veil of differentiation from one's own Self, directed toward things such as blue, yellow, pot, cloth, wall, mountain, river, and sky, which reside within the womb of Śiva and other states.

We shall demonstrate through the meaning of the middle peak (*madhyakūṭa*) that even in the impure path (*malinamārga*), such as *agrimāyā* and *prakṛti*, there exists an infinite range of objects to be desired and so forth, as well as the desire directed toward those objects, limited knowledge, and limited agency. In the pure path (*śuddhamārga*), the expansion of Īśāna consists of the nature of the fourth state (*turyarūpa*), whereas in the path of Māyā—
The expansion of Īśāna is by way of its impure form.
As it is said in the *Jñānārṇava*: "O Dear One, from the letter *Ī* arises this Viśvakartrī, whose nature consists of Māyā and Turyā.

All sacred fields (*kṣetra*), seats (*pīṭha*), pilgrimage sites (*tīrtha*), groves, forests, the earth, the Gaṅgā, and so forth—the vessel of Mahāmāyā born of the womb—is the meaning of the first peak-syllable, the letter *La*.

As it is said in the *Jñānārṇava*: "O Śivā, from the letter *la* arises the Goddess Earth, together with her mountains, forests, and groves; she is endowed with the fifty sacred seats (*pīṭhas*), consists of all holy fords (*tīrthas*), is supreme, consists of all the Gaṅgās, and consists of the locations of all sacred fields (*kṣetras*)."
The letter *la* here denotes Indra and also denotes the pure ground (*śuddhabhūmi*).
He expresses the very firmness of pure self-reflection by means of the seed-syllable of Māyā: *hnīṃ*.
Here, the syllable *hrīṃ* consists of the assembly of the sky (*vyoma*), fire (*vahni*), the long vowel (*dīrghasvara*), the half-moon (*ardhendu*), and the bindu.

Its meaning is as follows: that power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*)—through the letter *ha*, by its connection with Śiva whose nature is light, possesses the state of resting in the supreme space (*paramākāśa*); through the letter *ra*, it possesses the nature of the light of supreme illumination; and through the letter *ī*...

The state of being the agent of all is indicated by the half-moon (*ardhacandra*) through its nature as both pure and impure; the state of being the substratum for all matrices (*yoni*) is indicated by the drop (*bindu*); and the state of being the witness of all is indicated by the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*, which is distinguished by the *hara* (the letter *ha*), the *bindu*, and the *ardhacandra*. Thus, the meaning of the syllable *hrīṃ* is established. Here, this abundance of the pure path (*śuddhādhva-bhūmā*) flows.

The relationship of the concealed and the concealer exists as an objective reality; it is not merely a state established among the venerable masters and others regarding [objects such as] the thumb or the ritual vessel, but rather it is explained here as being present in all things.
Alternatively, the power (śakti) Ākāśeśvarī— *hrīṃ*, whose form is Māyā— is here the supreme Mahāmāyā, and not merely the limited Māyā found on the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*).
If it is asked how Mahāmāyā can have the nature of pure consciousness (*saṃvedana*), [the answer is that] this is evident in the following.
We maintain that this is because [the Lord] is the agent of the five: the Śāmbhava-śakti-mantra of Śivanātha, Maheśvara, Mantreśvara, and Mantra.

At the end of the first peak (kūṭa), by showing the syllable *hrīṃ* as if it were a lamp on a threshold, he indicates that in the preceding Śakyaṇḍa there is the nature of pure light (*śuddhatārūpa*) and greatness;
whereas in the subsequent [peaks], such as Māyā and Prakṛti, he makes known their very nature as illusion (*māyātva*), for above Māyā lies Mahāmāyā.

It is indeed said that she is celebrated as Śuddhavidyā; by this much, the cycle of recitation is completed, and thus the realization of the first peak-syllable, *oṃ ka dhra tri la hnīṃ*, is established.

(17) Now, if it is asked: "The full significance of the first seed-syllable *hrīṃ* has indeed been understood; however, what is the intention behind the middle and final ones? It is said: Listen with close attention as I determine the definitive conclusion of the Trika scripture, for I am intensely eager to establish the nature of Tripurā.

The threefold utterance of the syllable *hrīṃ* is for this purpose: [to signify] the Great Power named Tripurā, who resides in the city of Śiva and belongs to the venerable Lord Svacchanda; she is of the nature of both the supreme (*parā*) and the non-supreme (*aparā*), being the supreme-Śiva state in the luminous realm (*prakāśa-bhuvi*) and of the nature of the non-supreme in the lower realm (*adharadharā*) which is the human state (*nara-daśā*). She is the power of man (*nara-śakti*) situated in the city of Śiva.
She who effects the veiling of her own essential nature through the Aghora, Ghorāghora, and Ghora aspects— her own self-forms—
assumes the form of the three *kūṭas*.

The triad of causes characterized by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara; the triad of fires characterized by Dakṣiṇāgni, Gārhapatya, and Āhavanīya; the triad of powers characterized by majesty, energy, and counsel;
the triad of accents characterized by Udātta and the others; and the triad of states characterized by existence, non-existence, and that which transcends both.

The great mantra consists of twenty-four syllables and comprises three quarters; it is the triad of spaces consisting of the elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*), the mental space (*cittākāśa*), and the consciousness-space (*cidākāśa*); it is the triple stream of water consisting of the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and Sarasvatī; and it is the triad of austerities characterized by the physical, the vocal, and the mental.

The triad of internal organs known as mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), and ego (ahaṅkāra); the triad of individual souls characterized by Viśva, Taijasa, and Prajña; the triad of phonemes characterized by the letters U, M, and A; and the triad of vital breaths consisting of Prāṇa, Apāna, and Vyāna—as described in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.

She has encompassed her own self— the primary triangle characterized by will, knowledge, and action— which manifests the web of the universe as the three qualities (guṇas) characterized by sattva, rajas, and tamas, and as the three times characterized by past, future, and present; she has filled and protected it, having assumed the form of the secondary Trika within herself.

Within one's own self, Tripurākāmeśvarī should be contemplated again and again by means of the unfolding of the three *kūṭas*, so that through that [contemplation] there may arise identity with Her and the state of being Her beloved. The reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) beginning with *ka* and ending with *la* is *hrīṃ*, the *hṛllekhā*;
she is the power of supreme reflective awareness (*parā-vimarśa-śakti*) known as Tripurā.
Thus, the transformation beginning with *ha* and ending with *la* is that very [consciousness]; likewise, that which begins with *sa* and ends with *la* is also that very same [consciousness].
Indeed, there is nothing apart from this, because without the reflective awareness of consciousness (*cid-vimarśa*), the manifestation of the entire triadic class of phenomena would be impossible.
This is the meaning of the three seed-syllables: *hrīṃ*.
If it is asked, "How can the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* be a convention for the meaning of the Blessed Lady Kāmakalā?", we reply:

by the proclamation of the *Tripuropaniṣad*. Just as the *Tripuropaniṣad* declares that the supreme Blessed Lady Hṛllekhā, consisting of the syllable *hrīṃ*, dwells in every abode at the end of the three peaks (*trikūṭa*), she pervades all through her formidable power (*ghora*).

"This very same Blessed Lady is celebrated as Tripurā"—thus, the meaning of the mantra is that the entire universe consists of the three-born (*trikajāta*), and therefore everything has the form of Tripurā.
Because everything has the nature of Tripurā, it possesses a threefold character (*trikatva*); this was stated by the venerable Bhaṭṭārikā Kāmakalā herself.

In order to inspire confidence in the Great Queen regarding the venerable Śaṅkara, the preeminent teacher, it was proclaimed outside by means of the ritual of the child’s possession (*pratisvāveśa*), as follows: "The triad of the gods is the three Vedas of the fire-eaters"— thus is explained the verse recited in the liturgy.

"That very form is twofold— transcending the universe and consisting of the universe— and it is taught in the Trika scriptures as being colored by its own self-reflection (*vimarśa*). Thus, those pure ones who always contemplate the reality of the meaning of the Trika are known on earth as "Trikas"— those belonging to the Trika lineage— such as *Trikī* and others, even today.
They speak incorrectly.
The Trikas, established in the Kulasānas and devoted to the worship of the Kula, are renowned on earth as Kaulas who recite the Kulasūtras.
O Great Brāhmaṇa, those Bhaṭṭas known as Soddiṣṭābhaṭṭas, who possess the most excellent state of awakening, are remembered as Paṇḍitas (p.
19); those skilled in the application of mantras are called Rājānakas, whom people refer to as Raina.
Such is the detailed exposition on the determination of caste (*jātinirṇaya*); it should be consulted in the *Saṃhitā*.
Now, according to the maxim that "if Śiva is joined with Śakti, he is able to act; otherwise,
the Lord is certainly not capable even of a movement," in order to indicate the primacy of Śakti over the possessor of Śakti (the Śaktimat),
the meaning of the state of being a subject— beginning with the Mantramaheśvaras and so forth— is presented within the Pure Path.

And a small portion is now being examined. For instance: therein, first of all, by the Great Queen Bhaṭṭārikā, through her power of discernment (*vimarśa-śakti*), sovereignty—characterized by abiding in one's own essential nature as the light whose essence is mutual orientation toward Śivānātha, who is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*)—has been bestowed upon Rāmā, by virtue of whose grace [this occurs].
The designation "Supreme Lord" (Parameśvara) attained renown in the world; "Īśana" means sovereignty, which is synonymous with power (*śakti*) and capacity (*sāmarthya*).
Without the state of being a Lord (*īśāna*), the status of being a Lord (*īśvaratva*) would be untenable. Why?
Because supreme sovereignty arises from the exertion of the power of one's own self-reflection (*svavimarśa*); thus, one's own abiding state is supreme.

Otherwise, there would be a downward descent; therefore, consciousness devoid of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is not auspicious. Thus, even in the state of Sadāśiva-Īśvara within the *madhyamā* [channel], that reflective awareness which exists for Lord Śiva-Rāma—consisting of "I" and "this" according to the logic of two equal scales (*samadhṛtapuṭanyāya*)—is likewise the bestowal of a garland by the Queen, the Blessed Lady (*Bhaṭṭārikā*).
This was granted to him by Kāmakalā; however, in the form of Sadāśiva, the "this" (idam-aṃśa) is manifest as "I am this.

Because the "I" (aham-aṃśa) is dark due to the predominance of will (icchā), there is no impurity whatsoever. Even in Īśvaranātha, the "I" is dark, and in the form "this am I," it is precisely the portion of "this" that belongs to the portion of "I."
Due to this infusion (*niṣiñcana*), there is no stain whatsoever here either, by virtue of the majesty of the Queen of Reflection (*vimarśarājñī*). However,

even though in the state of the subject who is a Lord of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara-pramātṛdaśā*), this Lord Śiva perceives objects of knowledge as inherently distinct, nevertheless, he abides in the state of "I-ness" (*ahaṃbhāva*) grasped as pure consciousness alone (*śuddhacinmātra*).

If something has been taken away from a king without being given, one may seize another's property in relation to that [king]; just as, by means of that sovereignty consisting of supreme lordship, the power of discernment (*vimarśa-śakti*) belonging to the Lord Śiva is indeed *Śuddhavidyā*.
However, in the case of ordinary knowledge (*vidyā*), there is a slight impurity because it consists of the manifestation of the identity between "I" and "this."
The purity of the subject's power [is established].

While sporting with Śivanātha, he once turned his face outward; seeing the demon of the body in solitude, with its ten sense-organs as its heads, he became terrified. There, due to his own ninefold ignorance, he fell under the sway of Māyā, becoming excessively attached to the notion of "mine" regarding his family. Through the play of the fire of worldly existence, he became like a mere speck of gold.
Desiring a hundred [times more], he was made to abandon his goal for the sake of the multitude of worlds in the celestial realm by that Rākṣasa, like some other outcaste;

wandering there without reflection from here to there, deprived of noble lineage, birth, wealth, and refuge, those others who were tranquil and free from egoism were honored by him as ministers, even though they were capable of conquering the power of their own bodies. Jīvarāma alone remained.

The attainment of the state of self-reflection (*svavimarśa*) was heard from the discourse concerning his wife; through the true reflection born of association with the virtuous, he accumulated the power of his own innate energy (*svaśakti*). Since this compassion was shown by the Goddess toward Śiva, those *yātudhānas*—Rāvaṇa and others—who had caused wailing, suffering, and lamentation, met their dissolution within the splendor of Rāma, along with their bodies and all else.
We shall now explain the pair of middle peaks that indicate this intended meaning; therein, first, is the occasion for determining the middle peak.

Thus, although he possesses the ministerial power of discernment (*vimarśa-śakti*), the Lord Kāmeśvara— by virtue of the majesty of his own sovereignty whose nature is colored by manifold powers— having descended from the ground of the manifestation of the perfect "I-consciousness," binds himself like a silkworm in its cocoon and becomes a limited soul (*aṇu*).
(21) He recites the second *kūṭa*, which indicates autonomy and signifies that "the individual (*pudgala*) becomes a sacrificial animal (*paśu*"):
*hasakala hrīṃ*. In the middle *kūṭa*, which consists of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*) beginning with *māyā*, [he is] within the curtain of the sky abiding in his own nature;
by means of the power of self-concealment (*svatirodhāna-śakti*), he [is joined] with his consort, the power of the awareness of consciousness (*cid-vimarśa-śakti*).

Simultaneously, he accepts the state of being a limited subject (*pramātṛdaśā*), which involves playing together [with objects], abandons the reflective awareness of full subjectivity (*pūrṇāhantā*)—the thought "I know and I do all this"—and thereby becomes a knower (*jñātṛ*). In the state of internal entry into the limited body accepted as "mine" (*mamatā*), there arises the sense of "I" (*hasa*). Thus it is.

Reflecting thus, one realizes that through the forgetting of syllables— such as the letter *a*, the nasal bindu, and the visarga— one thinks "I know" and "I do all"; yet, by attaining the state of the Person residing within the heart, who is the size of a thumb,
one becomes the sustainer of the bodily machine bound by the cord of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), [emerging] from the heart-lotus in the form of the power of wind (*vāyu-śakti*).

The Kuṇḍalinī, residing in the region of the navel, having risen through the root-door as far as the End of the Twelve (dvādaśānta), becomes like a golden bud; [it purifies] the Āṇava-mala, which consists of the internal state of the thought "I am full," and the Māyīya-mala, which consists of the manifestation of differentiated objects of knowledge that constitute the external state.

The meaning is that "Ha" performs mere recitation (japa) within one's own self, which is inlaid with the impurity of karma consisting of the latent impressions (vāsanā) of the auspicious and inauspicious. In exhalation it is "Ha," and in inhalation it is "Sa"; thus one recites "Ahaṃ Saḥ" or "So'ham.

Even in that state, because there is no interruption in the reflective awareness (vimarśa) of the individual soul (aṇu), [the practitioner maintains] their own existence within both knowledge (vidyā) and ignorance (avidyā).
"Na jahāsyaho"—thus, through this hymn composed by the great devotees, his eternal *vimarśa* (reflective awareness) is reinforced.

Here too, he serves that Queen of *Vimarśa*, yet she remains concealed; for by the letter *ha* there is the reflective awareness of *prāṇa* in the form of the sun, and by the letter *sa* there is the reflective awareness of *apāna* in the form of the moon—here, too, there is light (*prakāśa*).
The existence of *vimarśa* (reflective awareness) resides in the syllable *ha*, and the existence of *prakāśa* (light) resides in the syllable *sa*. (p.

23) The existence of *vimarśa* and the light-and-awareness (*prakāśavimarśa*) are Śiva and Śakti; such is the nature of the two phonemes *ha* and *sa*. Thus, the *Tripuropaniṣad* states: "In this way, it is declared that [the supreme] consists of Śiva and Śakti; this is Śiva, the Supreme."

"Divine power (daiva) is this [state] of living; that which is the union of the sun and the moon is called 'that state' (tat-pada). Here, the letter *ha* is Śiva, and the letter *sa* is the living soul (*jīva*). Due to the connection between the prāṇa and apāna breaths, there is "hasa," or "haṃsa.
Even when reciting these two syllables, the meaning is that "that state" is said to be the locus of illumination (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
This [verse] states who is qualified for the recitation of the ajapā.

The syllable *ka* is the letter *k*, which signifies the vital breath (*prāṇa*). The meaning is that "ha" is the hearing of two syllables; for inhalation and exhalation are indeed the attributes of the vital breath. For the purpose of accepting the recitation as part of consciousness itself, it has been transformed into the state of the vital breath.
Prior consciousness was transformed into the vital breath; from this it is known that the vital breath is that [consciousness], and that vital breath is the downward-turned mind.

According to such scriptural passages, the letter *ha* is the external sky (*ākāśa*), while within, it is known as *sa*, existing in the form of the multitude of individual souls (*jīvavarga*). This multitude of souls is manifold, distinguished by categories such as gods, animals, and humans. Thus, these two syllables, *ha* and *sa*, have arisen as both the substratum and the superstratum; Brahman is that whose body is space (*ākāśaśarīram brahma*).

According to the Vedic scripture, "That indeed is fire, that is wind, that is the sun, that is the moon," and so forth, He has become manifold in form through the absence of the deficiency produced by the grasping of *māyā*. As the scripture states, "Indra, through his *māyās*, moves in manifold forms. Thus, through the medium of the mental dispositions (*bhāvanā*) of the multitude of individual souls (*jīva*), He appears as the Lord of Consciousness to the bound (*paśu*).
The acceptance of existence is the cause of independence.
That which is the supreme sovereignty of Maheśa, the accomplishment of the impossible, is the Goddess Māyā-śakti;
for it is said that she is the self-concealment of Śiva.

Now, if it is argued that even while in the state of a bound soul (paśubhāva), among the classes of living beings such as gods, animals, and so forth, there exists a mutual distinction between some individuals regarding the Lord’s act of ruling, knowledge, instruments, and play— and therefore all are equal— this is not so; listen.
(23) Regarding the secret instruction on consciousness: there is no distinction anywhere among all bodies;
therefore, by contemplating everything as consisting of that [consciousness], one becomes Bhairava.
That which is the nature of the Lord—whether will, knowledge, or action—is the entry into the specific [state] of the body and senses.
Whether it be the recitation of the *dvārāha* or the *ajapājapa*, or whether it be the moon or the sun,
from Lord Sadāśiva down to the smallest worm, insect, gadfly, mosquito, or ant, there is no distinction whatsoever among all these common beings.

Do you not hear the resonant beat of the drum of the Upanishads, which proclaims: "Vāsudeva is everything; all this is woven upon me like clusters of gems on a thread; know that those states which are sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa proceed from me alone"—by means of which you might forget the non-duality of Śiva?

Whatever will, knowledge, and action belong to Brahmā and the other [deities], those very same exist in even ants and other [creatures] by way of *vidyā* and *kalā*. Thus, this entire universe is composed of Śiva; for one who contemplates this, everything becomes [Śiva], and no contradiction arises. This very point is stated repeatedly even in the *Brahma-Mahārāmāyaṇa*.
"Whatever Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, Rudra, and the others perform everywhere as taught in the scriptures, contemplate thus:

'I, whose body is consciousness, do all that. If you ask why this is so, it is because that very same consciousness which resides in the sky of the sun—the ornament of the world of experience—is the same consciousness that dwells within the hollow interior of an insect."

Because of this difference, there is a mutual distinction among living beings with respect to their bodies, sense organs, and so forth: the gods and others possess bodies and sense organs composed of light (*tejomaya*), while mortals possess bodies, sense organs, and so on, composed of earth (*pārthiva*);
likewise, birds possess those composed of air (*vāyavīya*). This is because such a diversity of bodies and sense organs is observed.
Now, according to the principle that "one recites twenty-one thousand [breaths] day and night, constantly chanting 'haṃsa, haṃsa,
haṃsa' as the living soul," and since he thus mutters "so'ham" (I am He) throughout the day and night, what has become of him by which...?

(24) If it is argued that the cognizer desires the state of liberation because the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) "I am [this] everywhere" is easily attained, let it be so— if you know only this much, namely, that the Supreme Lord, the Master of Consciousness, dwells everywhere and at all times without distinction, then [the means] previously described are manifold...

The manifestation of fortunes accumulated through many births exists for one who stands near prosperity; you are blessed and have achieved your life's purpose. Therefore, in this very rest of consciousness, perform meditation, concentration, and the like—nothing else. As it was said by the sage Aṣṭāvakra: "If you remain having rested from the notion that there is something separate from the body..."

"Right now you shall become happy, peaceful, and liberated from bondage; likewise, this very bondage is beneficial as you practice meditative absorption (*samādhi*)," and so forth. These instructions on liberation find rest only in those whose hearts have been purified by the descent of grace (*śaktipāta*) through the independent Śaiva tradition and its observances, and not in others.
For indeed, regarding those who are vessels for the very lowest degree of grace, whether in the domain of knowledge (*vidyā*) or ignorance (*avidyā*),

they enter through the instruction of great secrets such as "I am," and so forth; since there is no other opening, those of dull faculties should exert themselves with diligence in the elaborations of speech to be described hereafter, as follows:
"The Self is to be known, it is to be heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon; for what will he do who does not know It?

Those who know It here sit together in peace"—and according to the principle that "the Vedas have as their subject matter those possessed of ignorance," [this applies] to such passages as "He, with fuel in hand, should approach a Guru who is learned in the Vedas and established in Brahman."

The teachings found in the *Smṛtis*, *Upaniṣads*, *Purāṇas*, and other such texts are to be accepted by qualified seekers of liberation (*mumukṣu*) for the purpose of awakening their own self-reflection (*svavimarśa*). Since instruction everywhere is intended solely for that purpose, pure self-reflection must be practiced by all qualified individuals, precisely for the sake of awakening one's own self-reflection, by means of the bestowing of supreme grace.
The *Nistaraṅga-upadeśa-śataka* (One Hundred and Twelve Waveless Instructions), spoken by the Supreme Lord himself in the *Vijñānabhairava*,
a treatise on yoga (*yogaśāstra*), for the sake of uplifting his own devotees, is of the *Śāmbhava* type.

By means of the Śākta and Āṇava upāyas. Among them, the first [verse] explains the three upāyas. As established by the verse "The vital breath (prāṇa) moves upward, while the individual soul (jīva) moves downward," if there occurs an act of reflective awareness (*vimarśana*)—either in the upward or downward state of the ascent and descent of the *prāṇa*—according to the path of the Guru's instruction, then liberation (*mokṣa*) [is attained].

"Since it has come into the hands [of the practitioner], it should be held right there. By this much, that is accomplished: within the space of the heart (*hṛdākāśa*), the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is established;

by the inclusion of the term "space" (*ākāśa*), its nature as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) is accepted by the Supreme Lord. That very state, which was attained during the recitation of the mantra, is expressed here as *hasaka*. In this regard:
Some maintain that because the letter *ka* expresses the meaning of the word "Self" (*ātman*), the Self should be understood as the individual soul (*jīva*) and the inner controller (*antaryāmī*).

Following the manifestation of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the letter *ha* is the essence of sound (*nādātman*); by means of the vocalization "I am He" (*so'ham*), it assumes the form of the unstruck sound (*anāhata*). That supreme state which resounds within the heart—that imperishable syllable (*akṣara*), we worship with reverence.

Thus it has been said: by some power or *kalā* that causes the forgetting of one's own self through the mere chanting of "haṃsa, haṃsa," one becomes as if unaware of one's own self— essentially like a mute, dull-witted, or inert person—
such that even after hearing the instruction of a true guru and the scriptures, one lacks the capacity for awakening due to being deluded by attachment toward unworthy objects.
That which has been described by the teachers through the medium of praise as the power of consciousness is that which does not attain the state of self-luminous manifestation within its own mouth.

Wherever the celestial beings, having been made to forget even their own selves by some portion of her through the power of the region of eternally surging, full-blown bliss, repeatedly remember that Self as if it were in another land— there, by means of hosts of infinite commands and even through the non-dualistic doctrines, the Supreme Goddess, who consists of both the transcendent and the immanent, triumphs.
He expresses the state of being like a mute snake by means of the syllables of the mantra.
The letter *la* is born as if insentient (*jaḍa*) due to the state of being a bound soul (*paśubhāva*); this is the meaning. (p.
26) Even in the two feet of the Great Mantra, it is the meaning of the two *kūṭas*. That is the light of the sun of awakening, experienced by all and exceedingly desirable.
On the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*) and in the state of *māyā* and so forth, while sporting through worldly convention (*vyavahāra*),
performing the process of ascent and descent, and even while offering praise to the Mantra, we meditate with the intellect— that is, with knowledge—
even through the recitation of the *haṃsa*; for though born from the great earth, the world, as one who was once insentient, he has become wise once again.

The meaning of the non-difference between the Śrīvidyā and the Gāyatrī is as follows: "May [the Goddess], abiding in her own essential nature, impel my powers of self-reflection (svavimarśa) along the pure path. Furthermore, the *Tripuropaniṣad* provides the following explanation for the word "dhīmahi":
"That syllable in which the quality of 'mahī'—meaning insentience (jaḍatva) or hardness (kāṭhinya)—is found is the syllable 'ma-hī' (the letter *la*)."

By this much, the meaning of the collection of syllables *hasaka-hala* is established as follows: the Lord Śiva, in the form of the two syllables *haṃsa*, is transformed into a state of insentience through the grasping of the state of the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) of sound, which is limited by the individual soul (*jīva*) within the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and space (*ākāśa*). This very dullness is explained as being the power *Hrīṃ*, the "Heart-line" (*hṛllekhā*).
"I shall act; Yadu, elsewhere [I am] like Śiva who has assumed the state of a beast"—thus is established this second contemplation of the peak-syllable (kūṭa).

Thus, up to the end of "tad āraty abharge," the contemplation (*vimarśa*) of the Pure Path (*śuddhādhvan*), which is intended as the meaning of the first *kūṭa*, has been applied. Immediately thereafter, up to "devasya dhīmahi," the intention of the second *kūṭa* was previously completed. Now, it is the occasion to apply the meaning of the third *kūṭa*, which is the meaning of the third part.

This very subtle state of the beast-like *pudgala*, whose master is bound by fetters, experiences once again—by its own absolute freedom (*svātantrya*) and following after that—the persistence of the manifestation of its own essential nature;
this is what is expressed by the third peak-syllable, *sakala hrīṃ*. Therein, the letter *sa* is the subject (*pramātā*), and by the desire for *ka*...

The literal meaning is that, by his own will, Lalitāsana once again became the Lord of all the gods, Cakreśvara. Alternatively, "he" refers to the one previously mentioned; even though he had attained a state resembling that of a swan through the recitation of the *haṃsa-mantra*, he forgot the extent of his own power and fell into a state of intermediate existence.

(p. 27) Even in such expressions as "Who am I? Who am I? it is he alone who has become a fit vessel for the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), having attained his own true nature through the power of his own grace.
Furthermore, by virtue of his awakened state, he incessantly contemplates "I am He, I am He," as the witness of all and the creator of all; such is the meaning of this statement.
The gurus have also taught [this] by means of verse.

Constantly and clearly muttering "I am He, I am He" throughout his own day and night, one who has forgotten the nature and power of the Lord of Sāmāya there falls into doubt by himself. But for one dwelling in awakening, the further certainty that arises—"Who am I? Who am I?"—is the very Sun of Consciousness itself, whose body is revealed as "I am He, I am He. Thus, you are yourself the Sun of Consciousness.

First there is the Great Light (*mahāprakāśa*), which is most pure; thereafter, in the state of Sadāśiva and so forth, it enters the stage of the "pure-impure. Then, having again entered the stage of the "impure" during the state of *māyā* by its own will, it becomes pure once more through the recognition of its own Self (*svātmapratyabhijñā*).
He says this very thing: "sakala hrīṃ."

Alternatively, "the whole" (*sakala*) refers to this entire sequence: the most pure, the purer, the pure-impure, the impure, and finally the state of being most pure; *hrīṃ* is that very power of Māyā previously mentioned—this is the meaning. Now, in the treatises on extraction (*uddhāra*), [it is said that] the *vidyā* is the *kāmakalā*.

If it is asked: "Why is there 'oṃ'? Why is there the recitation of 'ka dhra' and so forth, when only the sequence beginning with 'ka' is seen and not the sequence beginning with the *praṇava*?"—the answer is: True; the sequence beginning with 'ka' is seen with reference to the fifteen-syllable mantra, and this matter regarding the sixteen-fold [mantra] is also correct.
But surely, many other sixteenfold divisions have been described in various other ways?

The syllables *vāgbhava* and others, such as *lakṣmī*, *parā*, and *madana*, as well as the seed-syllable beginning with *māyā*, are placed at the beginning; thus, having placed [these] before the fifteenth [syllable], its state as the sixteenth is declared. When the author of the *Kalpalatā* says "hnīṃ dhnīṃ nlīṃ dhroṃ dhreṃ," if one of these seed-syllables is placed at the beginning of *trikuṭā* and so forth, then [the result follows].

If it is argued that all the *trikuṭās* consist of the syllables of *ṣoḍaśī*, and therefore one might ask why one should abandon any one of the fifteen vowels— such as *māyā*, *lakṣmī*, *kāma-bīja*, or *vāgbīja*— and instead adopt the *ṣoḍaśī* (sixteenth) vowel as the *praṇava* (the sacred syllable *om*), [the answer is] "amṛta" (nectar); thus, this is the *saṃhitā*.

(p. 28) Due to the authority of texts such as the *Pañcastavī*, the primacy of the *praṇava* (OM) is not intended in the Kādividyā. Indeed, in the *Saṃhitā*, this very position is adopted through the hymn to Queen Bhaṭṭārikā composed by the sage residing in La-hara-rāṣṭra, as follows: "The divine [Vidyā] beginning with KA, and that beginning with HA in the middle."

I have taken refuge in you, the Queen of Youth, who reveals the peaceful nature of the self through divine peaks, who transcends both effect and cause, and who is the primordial power (*śakti*). This description pertains to the Fifteenth [Vidyā]. As for the praises of the Sixteenth, they are as follows: [she is] the Supreme Elderly One (*parā vṛddhā*).
We have taken refuge in you, the Queen, the eternal one who is mounted upon Bhuvaneśī, who begins with the syllable *Tāra* (Om) from her three peaks,
and who is served by the twelve [deities] beginning with Śakra. We have sought shelter in you, the aged Sovereign.

The meaning is: [the goddess] Vṛddhā, who is mounted upon the sixteen-year-old Bhuvaneśī in the form of the syllable *hrīṃ*— that is, in the form of the *ṣoḍaśī* (sixteen-syllabled mantra) beginning with *hrīṃ ka e* and so forth— and who is enriched (*āḍhyā*) by the three peaks (*trikūṭaiḥ*), namely the *vāgbhava*, *kāmarāja*, and *śakti* peaks,
and likewise filled (*bharitā*) at the very beginning, prior to the first [syllables] such as *ka e ī*.

The meaning is: we praise her who is of many kinds, the sixteen-fold [Śodasī], whose nature is eternally the syllables *tārārṇa* (the Savior), *oṃ*, *aiṃ*, and *hrīṃ*. It is extremely well-known that the syllable *oṃ* is indeed the designator (*vācaka*) of *tārārṇa*. [She is accompanied by] Śakra and others, Śakra-kāma-lopa, Mudrā-manu, Candra, Kubera, Agastya, Nandi...

The sages Sūrya, Śaṅkara, Viṣṇu, and Durvāsas—by them, through the various distinctions of the desires of the twelve attendants (upāsakas) beginning with Śakra, there is the capacity for the differentiation of mantras; otherwise, how could it be so? [The sequence] is:
*kra* *la* *hnīṃ* *hra* *sa* *ka* *hra* *la* *hnīṃ* *sa* *ka* *la* *hnīṃ* ... [the sequence] of Indra’s worship is *kra* *la* *hnīṃ*.

Thus is the worship of Kāma: *hra sa kra la hnīṃ* and *hra sa ka hra la hnīṃ*. This is the recitation (*japa*) of Lopāmudrā: *kra hra dhra tra la hnīṃ*, *hra kra dhra tra la hnīṃ*, *sa hra ka dhra tra la hnīṃ*, *trargi*. The sequence of these and other variations should be investigated in such works as the *Kalpalatā*. In which...
A detailed exposition has been provided by us in due order; that very recitation of Durvāsas is supreme, yet it is devoid of the *oṃkāra*, the *bindu*, and the *nāda*.
As it is said: "That which is devoid of the *bindu* and devoid of the *nāda* shall be honored as the [mantra] of Durvāsas."

p. 29) *Kra dhra tra la hra rrī* and so forth; likewise, by the specific qualification "praised by Gaṇeśa and Vaṭuka," the *Ṣoḍaśī* within the *Praṇava* is indicated. Just as there exists a commentary on the *Pañcastavī* titled *Trikārthaviveka*, its commentator has explained it thus: "Gaṇeśa" means the Lord of the Gaṇas.

Mahādeva is indicated by the letter *ma*; Hari, in the form of a young ascetic (*baṭu*) or a dwarf (*vāmana*), is indicated by the letter *a*; and Brahmā, who is the primordial face, is indicated by the letter *ka*. By these, the letter *u* is indicated; thus, the aggregate of the letters *ma*, *a*, and *u* is the syllable *oṃ*. The meaning is that he is praised by this. Likewise, Kāma, whose companion is Rati, is the seed-syllable of desire, the letter *ka*.

"Endowed with that," and so forth. Here, by the instruction *ma-a-u*, the sequence of descent through the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭyavarohaṇa*) is well-established in this very manner. As it is stated in the *Brahmarahasya*: "The stainless [power], resembling the void, subtler than the subtle, supreme—beyond which one perceives the resonance (*nāda*); from the resonance, the power (*śakti*); from the power, the point (*bindu*)."
From the Moon (Candra) Prajāpati is born; from Prajāpati, Tejas is born; from Tejas, the origin of Rudra is born;
from Rudra, Viṣṇu is born; from Viṣṇu, Brahmā is born; and from Brahmā, the entire world—both stationary and moving—is born.
Thus, even though other letters may also denote [the same meaning], the excellence of the syllable Oṃ is established.

If it is argued that [the syllable] does not necessarily succeed in the *Kādividyā*, we say no; for in the *Ṛgveda* itself, the *ṣoḍaśī* is explicitly declared to be the *praṇava*. This is beyond doubt, because the word "knowledge" (*vidyā*) is indicated as being subordinate to the *oṃkāra*, just as in the passage:
"Desire, the womb, Kamalā, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the cave, laughter, the wind, the cloud, and Indra."
Furthermore, in the *Tripuropaniṣad*, it is stated: "The cave (*guhā*) is the letter *hrīṃ*; *sakalā* is the letter *sa*; this *purūṣī* is the primordial *vidyā* of the Mother of the Universe.
[Kāma is the letter *ka*; the womb (*yoni*) is the letter *e*; the single-streaked one (*ekamālā*) is the letter *ī*; Vajrapāṇi is the letter *la*; the cave (*guhā*) is *hrīṃ*;
Mātariśvan (the Wind) is the letter *ka*; day (*ahnaḥ*) is the letter *ha*; Indra is the letter *la*; the cave (*guhā*) is *hrīṃ*; and *sakalāḥ* is the letter *sa*.

The letters *ka* and *la*, along with *māyā* (*hrīṃ*) and *krauṃ*—this is the Vidyā of Kāmakalā, consisting of fifteen syllables. Though it is manifold and extensive, it is the Mother of the Universe, the progenitor of all.
How does it become sixteen syllables? To this, he provides a qualifying description containing the underlying reason: because... (p. 30)

"Ādividyā" means that at the beginning is the "Kādividyā"; she whose first knowledge (*vidyā*)—in the form of the *bindu* containing the realization—is the seed-syllable *Oṃ*, is the Ādividyā. Having placed the seed-syllable *Oṃ*, the source of knowledge, at the beginning, she becomes a sixteen-year-old maiden (*taruṇī*); this is the meaning. Now, one might ask: how can the word *vidyā* denote the syllable *Oṃ*?

Listen now to the Vedic statement: "Knowledge" (*vidyā*) means "realization" (*saṃvedana*). And this realization is of the nature of the *bindu*; indeed, the *oṃkāra* is of the very form of the *bindu*. Because it is said that "the *bindu* is realization without division," that *bindu* which consists of non-dual realization is alone the ultimate reality (*tāttvika*).

For it has been determined by the venerable Rāmakaṇṭha in his commentary on the verse "Oṃ tat sat" within the *Sarvatobhadra* that the syllable *oṃ*, known as the *praṇava*, is indeed of the nature of the light of consciousness (*citprakāśarūpa*).

If it is asked, "What is the meaning of consciousness that is devoid of division? it is said: that light which is the very nature of consciousness is the syllable *oṃ*. Although light is twofold—by way of being transcendent of the universe and by way of being identical with the universe—it nevertheless denotes Brahman alone, according to the principle that "the *praṇava* is the designator of that. Thus, the status of being a designator also belongs to the *praṇava*.

In its form as words (*pada*) and its form as sentences (*vākya*), it possesses the nature of a word through the power of the whole (*samudāya-śakti*) as that which transcends the universe, and the nature of a sentence through the power of the parts (*avayava-śakti*) as that which consists of the universe. In this regard, with respect to the sentence, there is distinctness (*vyastatva*); with respect to the word, there is totality (*samastatva*). Therein lies the triad of words that is independent.

The characteristics of the letters *ā*, *u*, and *ma* constitute that very sentence. Within that, the *oṃkāra*—which consists of the *bindu* whose nature is the cognition of differentiation—is the gross three-measure (*mātrā*) form of the word.

The knowledge of differentiation belonging to the letter *u* consists of the *Ṛgveda*, the waking state, and the element *Bhūḥ*, having Brahmā as its essence. That of the letter *a* consists of the *Yajurveda*, the dream state, and the element *Bhuvaḥ*.
The form of Viṣṇu; the deep sleep of the Sāmaga singers as the syllable *ma*; the heaven-world (*svarloka*) consisting of Rudra;
and the proclamation of the differentiation of that which consists of the universe—this is the meaning of the syllable *oṃ*.

With the intention of expressing that [reality] which consists of the universe and is Brahman, there is the realization of the dissolution of the distinctions between phonemes such as *a* and the others.

The *praṇava* makes known even Brahman, which transcends the universe and is undivided; it makes known the entire, undivided nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) through the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) consisting of the abandonment of the literal parts. Thus, in the state of non-differentiation, the *bindu*, whose essence is pure awareness, is the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*).

Now, one might object: "Since the three gross *mātrās* of the syllable *oṃ* signify the consciousness that consists of the universe (*viśvamaya*), what need is there for it to be connected with *mātrās* that transcend the universe? [The answer is:
Its form is constituted by its own subtle portion, characterized as the half-*mātrā*, which takes the form of the *bindu*.
We maintain that this is because of its demonstration.

With the intention that this very form of Oṃkāra—consisting of the experience of non-differentiation and known as the *bindu*—is its ultimate reality, the Blessed Lord said: "The designation of Brahman is threefold: Om, Tat, Sat."

The meaning of the *praṇava* as the designator of Brahman is established as follows: the meaning of the letter *U* is consciousness (*caitanya*) conditioned by the subtle phenomenal world (*sūkṣma-prapañca*); the meaning of the letter *A* is consciousness conditioned by the gross phenomenal world (*sthūla-prapañca*);
and the meaning of the letter *M* is consciousness conditioned by the power of *māyā*, which is the cause of both the gross and subtle forms.

The meaning of *vāśya* is pure consciousness (*caitanya*) alone, attained by abandoning the gross and subtle parts of phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca*) as well as their cause, *māyā*. This is the meaning of *vāśya* as the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*). Even that [half-measure] is abandoned along with its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), leaving only the indicated object (*lakṣya*), which is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). Thus, because these four have a single substratum, they are one—perfect and pure.

It is established that Brahman as pure consciousness is the meaning of the syllable *oṃ*; furthermore, the claim that "knowledge" (*vedana*) and the "point" (*bindu*) are merely synonyms for *oṃ* is true.

If this is so, then it follows that the doctrine of pure consciousness (*vijñānavāda*) results [from this], since, in effect, the knowledge of distinctions alone is what is to be meditated upon because of its subtlety. This is true, even though...

Although consciousness itself is subtler than all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), nevertheless, by designating it as "the denoter" (*vācaka*) of that [consciousness], it makes known the consciousness as the denoter and the cognizer as the most subtle; however, it does not indicate an independent consciousness, because consciousness finds its rest in the cognizer. Therefore, for this reason as well...

The Self, characterized as the knower (*saṃveditṛ*), is self-luminous, most subtle, and the object of worship; it is that which rests solely in pure consciousness. Although even a subtler awareness—dependent on the body and mediated by action—is somehow inferred, [the Self] is defined as the knower, the experiencer, and the cognizer.
The eternal Supreme Lord is never inferred [as an object].
In that regard, knowledge is self-established; whereas action, being dependent on the body, may be perceived by others, and through it, other knowledge is inferred.

Because it has been stated, "O Maitreyi, by the One through whom the knower is known," the previous Guru, having realized that knowledge— which is more subtle— comes to rest in the most subtle Knower, became a teacher of this intent; thus,
for the sake of the meaning "Salutation to the Great Aṇu, even beyond the upper half-mora of the Praṇava," he [uttered] the *Sārasvata*.

The author of the hymn also establishes that the syllable *akṣara* denotes Brahman: "O Sarasvatī, you who encompass the three Vedas, the three meters, the three worlds, and even the three gods through the three letters beginning with *a*; you who, transcending all modifications, pervade the fourth state (*turīya*) with your subtle sounds; you who hold everything both collectively and individually—I bow to you."
And one should chant "Om" as the sacred word, even in the secret scriptures.

With reference to the Great King, the Supreme Lord whose characteristic is consciousness (*saṃvedṛ-lakṣaṇa*), the description is made of the perception of the form of *Oṃ* as being the seat (*pīṭha*). For indeed, having occupied the seat by some Great King or other, there arises that which is independent: the lotus with six petals; and of that [lotus], it is the womb called the pericarp (*karṇikā*).

That which is the threefold cavity in the belly is the seat of the syllable Oṃ; within that, I continuously meditate upon the Mother of All, who is dark-hued, bowed by the weight of her breasts, and has emerged from Kuṇḍalinī.
Now, one might object: "In the *Pañcastavī*, the *praṇava* is taught as the aggregate of the syllables *a*, *ā*, and *u*;

since it is likewise indicated in the *Brahmarahasya*, why is there this distinct teaching elsewhere—namely, that first comes *a*, then *u*, and then *m*? To this it is replied: [this is for the sake of] the *Pāñcarātras*.

The pronunciation is intended to follow the sequence of the forms of the syllables *u*, *m*, and *a*. Having transcended the state of the Pradyumna-vyūha— the Creator (Vidhātṛ) who is Brahman and whose nature is the unfolding of volition (*saṅkalpa*)—
and likewise having transcended the syllable *ma*, which is of the nature of Rudra, the Aniruddha-vyūha, and characterized by tamas;

Since union with Vāsudeva, whose nature is the primordial material cause (*paraprakṛti*), is the goal to be attained, there is a convention in his system at the time a child begins to learn the alphabet: *u*, *sa*, *o*, *oṃ*.
These correspond respectively to the earth element (*pṛthvī-tattva*), the primordial material cause (*prakṛti-tattva*), and their presiding deities, Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, and Viṣṇu.
Having transcended the state of *māyā* (p.
42) and ascended through the stages of the principles (*tattva*) of *śuddhavidyā*, *īśvara*, *sadāśiva*, and *śakti*,
because union with *paramaśiva* is the desired goal, as for that which...
The venerable feet of the renunciant Madhusūdana Sarasvatī have demonstrated that the meaning of the letter *a* is the *Ṛgveda*, the waking state, the earth, and the nature of Brahmā;

the meaning of the letter *u* is the *Yajurveda*, the dreaming state, the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), and the nature of Viṣṇu; and the meaning of the letter *m* is the *Sāmaveda*, deep sleep, heaven, and the nature of Rudra—this being for the purpose of clarifying the sequence *a-u-m*. That too [is correct].

This should be understood with reference to the view of the Paurāṇikas, for in the Purāṇas the manifestation of creation is described in this very sequence: first Nārāyaṇa, thereafter Viriñci is born from his navel, and following that, Mahādeva is born from his forehead. This...
The sequence of descent according to the venerable Lord is, in that system, the convention regarding the child: *a, u, ma, o, oṃ*.
By this much, this is merely the knowledge; however, that knowledge which is of the nature of the *vidyā-bindu* is the *oṃkāra*.
Thus, having placed the *oṃkāra* at the beginning, the first [mantra] is established as the *ṣoḍaśī* of the fifteen-day period.

Through the utterance of the *praṇava*, may the Goddess—the fifteen-syllabled Mahārājñī and the sixteen-syllabled one—protect Śiva from the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). This sixteen-syllabled [mantra] is the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) whose nature is that of the knower;
for it is non-different from Nārāyaṇa, according to the Vedic revelation: "Since there is nothing other than this."

Because there is no other born being superior to Him who has entered into all worlds—Prajāpati, in harmony with His progeny, [is] those three lights and He is the sixteenth; herein the meaning is this:
from that Light whose nature is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), there is no other born being, nor any other being being born.

There is no other category superior or more excellent than the object of cognition (*prameya*) and so forth; because objects of cognition and the like are insentient, they are inferior due to their dependence on another. That Prajāpati, the supreme subject who, upon being born, exercises his volition, has entered into all worlds—that is, he has permeated them—by virtue of bestowing existence upon everything.

Because he is all-pervasive, he alone is the Lord of all; through *prajā*—that is, through desire (*kāma*) consisting of the letter *ka*, which is the lineage of the power of will—he makes everything conscious. (p.
43) He [perceives] the three lights characterized by the sun, moon, and fire, which constitute the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of knowledge (*prameya*).

These [objects] consist of the knower, and he perceives them through the relation of inherence (samavāya). For the Śruti declares: "In whom the heaven, the earth, and the mid-region are woven together with the vital breaths and all else. They say that the Sun is the means of knowledge (pramāṇa), they declare the Moon to be the object of knowledge (meyam), and this Fire is the supreme reality (paraṃ tattvam).
"This belongs to the knower" — such is the statement in the *Tantrāloka*.
Moreover, when Prajāpati— Viṣṇu in the form of Śiva at the time of the burning of Tripura— unites with the three lights,
the three peaks consisting of the fifteen letters beginning with *ka*, *e*, and *ī*, which are the three peaks (*kūṭa*) composed of clusters of phonemes,
he becomes present within them; that very Lord is the imposition [of identity] as "the sixteenth is the face, the moon."

The sixteenth is of sixteen-fold form; it consists of the pure vital breath, ether, air, fire, water, earth, the senses, mind, food, vigor, austerity, mantra, action, world, name, and form— it is of the nature of *māyā* in the form of the Puruṣa of sixteen parts, for this divine power of mine is composed of the qualities (*guṇas*).

Since it is stated that [Māyā] is difficult to transcend, its nature as the sixteen-syllable [mantra] indicates that it is the form of Viṣṇu’s Śakti. Thus, because Vimarśa-Śakti and Nārāyaṇa are non-different and constitute half the body of Paramaśiva,
their mutual state of *sāmarasya*— the state of being a *lolībhāva* or blending— is the *yāmala*, which is the *saṅghaṭṭa*.
Thus it is said; and likewise, in the *Bṛhatkathāsaritsāgara*, Mahādeva speaks to the Goddess:
"Since he [Viṣṇu] is born from half of my body, and since you yourself are Nārāyaṇa, you are indeed my power (*śakti*), while I am the possessor of power (*śaktimant*);
from that time forth, this twofold form of mine has been renowned."

"The form of Ardhanārīśvara, the body that steals half of Hara's head—therefore, O Hari, I grant eternal nature and my own state to my devotees. This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the Śāktas: that there is *sāyujya* (union) with Viṣṇu. Furthermore, in the passage "O Govinda, the Goddess who is your sister grants that state at the end," it is Mahāmāyā-Śakti herself who is the very essence of Viṣṇu.
The Blessed Lord himself reveals his own *māyā* in the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*: "O Radiant One, men [worship] you, the sovereign lady of all desires and boons.
(p. 44) *aciṃṣmantīṃ manuṣyās tvāṃ sarvakāmavareśvarīm*.
Bestowing the boon of all desires through offerings of incense, oblations, and sacrifices, men on earth establish names and shrines for her:
as Durgā, Bhadrakālī, Vijayā, Vaiṣṇavī,
Kumudā, Caṇḍikā, Kṛṣṇā, Mādhavī, Kanyā, Māyā, Nārāyaṇī, Śoṇā, Śāradā, and Asvikā.

The names [of the villages] are explained by their very utterance; the locations, such as Bālāśrama, Tūlamūlya, Ṣoḍaśīgrāma, and so forth, are well known. The manifestation of Trikūṭa is as described in the Saṃhitā:
As the high-souled Bhairava was burning Tripura,
he drew his excellent bow toward the Himalaya with his splendor,
for the purpose of fixing the arrow and discharging it.
The light produced from Viṣṇu was originally threefold;
that very light manifested from the shaft (śalya) and became the river flowing through the three paths (Tripathagā).
Furthermore, the flame that arose during the act of holding [the arrow] is celebrated as Bālā.
The flame that is being drawn forth is proclaimed as the "Young Woman" (Bālā);
the flame that rises upward is proclaimed as the "Aged One" (Vṛddhā). O lady of excellent complexion, she has gone from Bālā to Lohapura in Pātāla.
O Īśvarī, the young woman went to the city of Jvālāpura,
while the old woman, the great Jvalā, went to the golden city; in one moment the flame departed, and in one moment she reached the three cities.
Having reduced [the cities] to ashes, she remained there pervading the entire universe; thus it is determined that this Vaiṣṇavī power, known as Tripurā, is Mahāmāyā.

Just as she pervades the entire universe by way of the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), so too the Queen, the Mother of all beings, consists of the universe even in the form of the letters of the *Kāmakalā-vidyā*. Thus,
the meaning of the three *kūṭas* has been shown in another manner by the Lord Maheśvara Bhaṭṭāraka himself in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*, as follows:
O Supreme Goddess, O Beloved, listen with attention to how the entire universe is pervaded by the primordial Vidyā consisting of Śiva, Śakti, and the rest;
the universe is composed of the five elements, and that eternal [Vidyā] is identical with it.
And the root-vidyā consisting of that [syllable]—I shall describe it likewise.

From the letter *ha* arises space (*vyoma*), from the letter *ka* comes the wind (*prabhañjana*), from the letter *ra* comes fire (*agni*), and from the letter *sa* there is the origin of the water-element (*jalatattva*).
From the letter *la*, the earth (*pṛthivī*) is born; therefore, she (the earth) consists of the entire universe.
Fifteen qualities are proclaimed to belong to the elements; Śivā is composed of them.
Whatever power is said to belong to whichever object, that very power is the Goddess, the Sovereign of All, and that very object is Maheśvara, the Great Lord.
Pervaded by fifteen syllables, that Vidyā consists of the qualities of the elements;
likewise, through five, six, and four syllables,
distinguished by vowels and consonants, she embodies the thirty-six principles (tattvas).
And this vidyā, whose nature transcends the [lower] principles, has been cultivated as eternal;

this is the intended meaning here: the state of equilibrium between Śiva and Śakti is manifestation (prakāśa) and reflective awareness (vimarśa), and by the previously mentioned method, that very manifestation and reflective awareness, having become condensed, exists as the five elements.
The syllables of those elements, beginning with the letter *ha*,

transform by becoming dense with both light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); thus, within the triad consisting of the five elements whose nature is Śiva and Śakti, there are the phonemes, and the Goddess Kāmakalā is composed of that entire universe.

The meaning is "having entered into another. Through the relationship of the pervaded and the pervader among the five elements, there come to be fifteen qualities. For instance, among space and the others, each preceding one is the pervader and each succeeding one is the pervaded.
Space has one quality, namely sound; air has two, namely sound and touch.
Fire possesses sound, touch, and form; water has four qualities—sound, touch, form, and taste;

earth has five—sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. Thus, there are fifteen qualities in the Great Elements (*mahābhūta*), and the venerable Goddess (*bhaṭṭārikā*) likewise has exactly fifteen phonemes, beginning with *Vāgbhava*.

The five *kūṭas* beginning with *kra dhra tra* belong to the *kāmarāja*; the six beginning with *rhra? sā?* are related to the *śakti-kūṭa*; and there are four beginning with *sā?* [belonging to the *vāmācāra*]. Thus, the *saubhāgyavidyā*, consisting of fifteen syllables and composed of the five elements (*pañcabhūta*), belongs to whomever it may be.

Whichever power belongs to any object, that is the Sovereign of All; and that which is all is the Great Lord—by this determination, the entire universe consists of Śiva and Śakti; such is the meaning of the three seed-syllables (kūṭatraya).

Even by Śiva, in the form of the author of the Vivaraṇa, this very same point has been stated in a different manner; for whatever small measure of benefit exists therein, the sole cause is the compassionate glance of the independent Supreme Lord, which bestows even a mere fragment of the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
It should be forgiven by those excellent masters of lay practitioners (*upāsaka-guruvara*) that this [work] was composed for us; may it be pleasing to them.

Om! This King of Mantras has been explained by one named the Kashmiri Upādhyāya Viśuddhaśivasvāmin, whose mind was purified by bathing in the Vitastā and Gaṅgā rivers meeting at the mountain forests of Ārūra.
The tradition of the manifest, stainless, and true lineage is the supreme Śrī; from that mountain, which is like a white stone, beginning from its very descent—so much is meant.
This commentary on the mantra is complete.
